Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education
and Cultural Affairs. My name is Becky Smith, and I am providing testimony in opposition to LD 1759,
An Act to Allow Firefighters to Be Eligible for State College Funding on behalf of the Maine Community College System.
As this committee well knows, the funds deallocated from Maine's Free College Program in this bill are, in fact, already committed to pay for Maine's current free college students. This is why the funding was
included in LD 609, the "Part A" budget. Due to the overwhelming success of the Maine Free College
program, all of these funds are needed to support the commitment made by the 1315` Legislature.
This committee may be less familiar with the Maine Fire Service Institute (MFSI), authorized in statute (Title 20-A, Chapter 319, �9001) administered by Southern Maine Community College and run primarily from the Brunswick campus. Bills that affect MFSI are generally heard in the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee which is why a $200,000 allocation to MFSI garnered unanimous support
in their biennial budget recommendation to the Appropriations committee.
However, I wanted to share this bit of history with you:
Maine Fire Service Training, now known as Maine Fire Service Institute, began its journey in 1958 as a division ofthe Maine Department ofEducation and is now a department ofSouthern Maine Community College. It came to be because a group of dedicated individuals and groups were able to come together for the benefit ofMaine 's firefighters and citizens. It was governed by an advisory committee made up of Maine fire chiefs, members of the Maine Federation of Firefighters, insurance underwriters and other municipal and Department of Education members, quite similar to the advisory committee of today. These members were appointed by their respective organizations and were groundbreakers that not only realized the need to train Maine 's firefighters but also to train their oflicers in the areas offirefighting tactics, administration and leadership. This group 's highest priority was not the number of students trained but the quality of the education they received, a mission we still hold today.
If you are interested in learning more, please visit their website or read their latest newsletter.
MFSI has an Advisory Committee comprised of fire chiefs from across the state, from both municipal and volunteer departments, the Maine State Federation of Firefighters, The Professional Fire Fighters of

Maine, MEMA, DOL, Risk Management, the SMCC President, The State Fire Marshall, staff of MFSI
and presently, Senator Chip Cuny.
MFSI is proud to provide a full range of certification training throughout the state in partnership with municipal and volunteer fire departments. MFSI provides not only training, train--the-trainer programs,
administers certification exams and loans out props and training equipment but also goes to the location
of the training need.
We know that MFSI, like many of our programs, is resource and staff constrained. In an ideal world, we
would be here supporting a bill that creates dedicated positions and includes ongoing funding. The program, like our seven community colleges needs ongoing consistent financial support.
However, this bill which takes one-time funds that benefit the youngest MFSI students and others
training to be EMS providers, nurses, plumbers, cybersecurity experts and childcare providers is not
something we can support.
We recommend that the committee vote "Ought Not to Pass" on LD 1759. Thank you.

Testimony ofRep. Benjamin Hymes
LD 1759, "An Act to Allow Firefighters to Be Eligible for State College Funding99
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs

April 28, 2025
Good morning, Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and members of the Joint
Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs. My name is Representative Benjamin Hymes, and I proudly represent House District 38. I am here to present LD
1759, "An Act to Allow Firefighters to Be Eligible for State College Funding" .
Last year, when OSHA considered stricter regulations, it became clear that many
municipalities struggle to ftmd basic firefighter training. The potential for massive budget
shortfalls in Maine's firehouses sparked my search for a better funding solution--one that
would also help ease the growing municipal tax burden.
Supporting firefighter education should be a top priority. The cost of training a firefighter is comparable to just one semester hour of college, yet the return-----the ability to save a home, a vehicle, or a life--is priceless.
Importantly, this bill does not request new appropriations. It simply redirects existing
education funds to the Fire Services Institute to cover the cost of firefighter training
statewide.
I would respectfully suggest amending the bill title to better reflect its intent: "An Act to
Fund Firefighters' Education."
Thank you for your time and consideration. I would be happy to answer any questions.

Benjamin Hymes
State Representative

Thank you Mr. Chair, Senator Joe Rafferty, Madam Chair Kelly Murphy, and the esteemed members of The Education and Cultural Affairs Committee. I am Representative Mike Lance of district #79 (Paris, West Paris, Sumner and Woodstock), I am also a member of the Paris Fire Department.
I am here to speak in support of Representative Hyme's bill, LD- 1759, "An Act to Allow Firefighters
to Be Eligible for State College Funding" .
A little about my fire service. I am a per-diem firefighter, meaning I have a pager and radio and
respond when I am available (the station is 4 minutes down the road). I started with BLS (Basic Life
Support), but I now have EVOC (Emergency Vehicle Operating Course), Interior Attack, Hazmat,
Extraction, Ladders, and Ambulance Assist training. Last year, Paris Fire had 502 call-outs. While fire training is essential, only a small percentage of the calls were fires. In addition to grass and structure fires,
I also worked:
lift assists
car accidents
CO alarms
smoke detectors
welfare checks
flooded basements
We do it all and our training has to be diverse. Like other small towns in Maine, we provide mutual aid
with 3 other towns: West Paris, Oxford, and Norway. All of the training I have received has been through
grants, other departments, my department and "on the job" . I would have greatly benefitted attending the
Maine Fire Service Academy.
This bill would help remedy one of the greatest problems we have in Maine right now regarding public
safety, the lack of well-trained first responders.
This bill reduces one-time funding provided in Public Law 2025, chapter 2 for the State's 7 community
colleges to continue offering student scholarships through the State's free community college tuition
program for eligible persons who graduate high school or obtain the equivalent of a high school diploma
in 2024 or 2025 by $800,000 in fiscal year 2025-26 and appropriates $800,000 on a one-time basis to the
Maine Fire Service Institute. It is my belief that many young people in my community and state wide
would commit to this profession if they had the financial assistance for the training necessary. I strongly urge you to vote, "ought to pass" on this critical bill. I will try to answer any questions you might have.

Proudly Serving House District 72 Paris, Sumner, West Paris, Woodstock

LETTER FROM THE DIRECTOR

FACING THE FIRE SERVICE OF TOMORROW -- TOGETHER

April 25, 2025

Dear Maine Fire Service Professionals,
The modern fire service is standing at a crossroads.
Today's challenges aren't iust about fires, motor vehicle crashes, or medical calls. They're about preparing the next generation to handle all of it--and to do so with the knowledge, skill, and professionalism that today's fireground and legal environment demand. But we're seeing a troubling
trend emerge with the "right now generation"--a growing impatience with process, a desire for immediate results, and at times, a lack of appreciation for the depth of responsibility that comes with wearing the badge of a fire officer.
At the Maine Fire Service Institute, we know that meaningful training takes time. It takes careful planning, review, and alignment with evolving NFPA standards--many of which change every five
years. Each change must be studied, absorbed, and reflected in our curriculum. That's not something you rush if you care about quality. That's something you build. And we're building it with purposeMaine purpose.
Our programs aren't cut-and-paste national templates. They carry real Maine flavor. That means when you're serving as a fire officer and responding to incidents, you aren't iust thinking about how to stretch a line or run a command board -- you're thinking about Maine law. You know when to notify
the State Fire Marshal's Office. You know how to engage with Inland Fisheries & Wildlife, DEP, DHHS,
Maine Forest Service and more-because missing a step in that process can land your department in legal hot water faster than any fire ever will.
Let's be crystal clear: ignorance of the law or operating standards is not an excuse in today's fire
service. When you're in a position of responsibility, you're expected to know your job--and do it well.
MFSI is committed to giving you every tool to succeed, but it's up to each of us, individually and collectively, to embrace the commitment to train hard and train right.
We need to raise the bar in fire sen/ice training across Maine--not lower it for convenience. This is
about protecting each other, our departments, and the people we serve. It's about building a future
where the next generation is not only capable, but confident, competent, and fully prepared for the realities they will face. So let's stay the course. Let's be patient where patience is required. And let's
never stop demanding excellence of ourselves and those who stand beside us.
Train hard. Train smart. And never forget who's counting on us.
With the highest of respect, and a reminder to be safe when the bell sounds, we need you all.
Jimmy

LD 1759, An Act to Allow Firefighters to Be Eligible for State College Funding
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, my name is Shawn Esler, and it is a privilege to serve as the State Fire Marshal.
I write in opposition of LD 1759.
While the Department of Public Safety supports fire service training, LD 1759 does not provide ongoing funding necessary to conduct sustainable firefighting programming.
The Maine Fire Service Institute (MFSI) is authorized in statute (Title 20-A, Chapter 319, �9001) and is administered by the Southern Maine Community College. MFSI is considered Maine's authority on fire service training and supports fire departments across the State. MFSI delivers training, certification exams, guidance, train-the-trainers, and lends out advanced fire training props. Recently, MFSI and the FMO partnered to deliver fire investigation training in Bangor and Portland. We fully intend to strengthen that partnership in the coming years.
It is my understanding that these funds are already allocated to current students. These students are likely to include those enrolled in an emergency medical technician program, which is a prerequisite in most fire departments for those students looking to apply for a career in firefighting. Additionally, most fire science associate's degree programming occurs in the Community College System. Reducing those funds may have unintended consequences. In essence, these funds are already being utilized to support Maine's firefighters.
While this bill is well intended, I would ask you to consider a bill that creates dedicated positions at MFSI and one that includes ongoing financial support. Maine is facing emerging risks in the fire service. More training is required to prepare the next generation of emergency responders.
I ask you vote "Ought Not to Pass" on LD 1759 and consider a different funding source.

___________________________ Shawn Esler, State Fire Marshal
